mcqs.question: Why are Moore machine outputs inherently glitch-free within a clock cycle?
options: Because the output is a pure function of the current state, and state only changes at clock edges, so output can't react to a mid-cycle input change
Because Moore machines have no inputs at all
Because Moore machines run at a slower clock speed
Because Moore machines don't use combinational logic anywhere
mcqs.explanation: Since a Moore machine's output depends only on state (not directly on input), and state is held in flip-flops that only update at clock edges, the output cannot change mid-cycle in response to a noisy or changing input -- unlike Mealy, where output is combinational on the input.

mcqs.question: What is a practical advantage a Mealy machine can have over an equivalent Moore machine?
options: It can never glitch, unlike Moore
It can react to an input within the same clock cycle and sometimes needs fewer states for equivalent behavior
It doesn't require any flip-flops to implement
Its outputs never depend on the current input
mcqs.explanation: Because a Mealy machine's output is a combinational function of both state and input, it can respond within the same cycle an input arrives, and can sometimes encode distinctions Moore would need an extra state to represent -- at the cost of potential output glitches if the input is noisy.

mcqs.question: What is the main trade-off between binary and one-hot state encoding?
options: One-hot always uses fewer flip-flops than binary
Binary encoding cannot represent more than 4 states
Binary uses fewer flip-flops (log2(n) for n states) but can need more complex next-state decode logic; one-hot uses one flip-flop per state but often has simpler, faster per-state logic
One-hot encoding is only usable in Mealy machines, never Moore
mcqs.explanation: Binary encoding minimizes flip-flop count but requires decoding a binary pattern to determine 'which state', adding logic complexity. One-hot trades more flip-flops (one per state) for simpler, faster per-state logic, since 'am I in state X' is just reading one dedicated bit.
